newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic calls for reforms, reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic calls for reforms, reshuffle.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, fighting off pressure at home and abroad, called on Thursday for economic reforms, a cabinet reshuffle and settling of political disputes in a democratic manner.

"The success of overall economic policy depends largely on personnel who will implement it in state bodies as well as in economy and finances. This implies an appropriate government reshuffle," state news agency Tanjug quoted him as saying after meeting Serbian Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic.

Milosevic is facing the biggest challenge to his 10-year-old rule after his ruling socialists annulled opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition victories in 14 of Serbia's 18 biggest cities, including Belgrade.

The fraud, confirmed by a fact-finding mission of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, prompted up to half a million people to protests in the streets of Belgrade and elsewhere across Serbia for nine weeks.
Milosevic, locked in a bitter power struggle between the moderates and hardliners, has not yet spoken out on the internal conflict or the confrontation with the opposition.
The cabinet reshuffle, in which Marjanovic was seen as likely to be replaced, has been widely rumoured as imminent as a result of the infighting.
Diplomats believe the composition of the new cabinet would be a strong indication of who was gaining the upper hand.
In the main evening newscast on Wednesday, state television showed Milosevic together with Marjanovic and several other rival political leaders.
Diplomats and analysts finely tuned to the intricacies of Serbian politics believe the television footage was meant to signal that differences have been smoothed out, at least for the time being.
Marjanovic informed Milosevic on preparations for structural and ownership changes in the republican economy, Tanjug said.
"The preservation and strengthening of political stability of the country is of enormous importance for Serbia," Tanjug quoted Milosevic as saying.
The statement, according to Tanjug, was conciliatory as Milosevic came under increasing pressure by the West which, spearheaded by the United States, has sharply condemned his conduct.
Washington has threatened further sanctions against Belgrade unless it improves its human rights record.

Washington's continuing sanctions, postponement of the European Union's restoration of Belgrade's preferential trade status and a halt in talks on Yugoslavia's readmission to the International Monetary Fund, have badly affected the already shattered economy, desperately needing fresh foreign capital.
The OSCE on Thursday once again told Milosevic he must fully recognise Zajedno's local election wins.
In Strasbourg, the European Parliament urged the European Union and its individual countries to freeze relations with Serbia until it undertook democratic reform.
Milosevic admitted the protracted political crisis was hurting the country and struck a rare conciliatory tone.

"The confrontations which have taken place on account of political differences are causing the country not only political but also great economic damage and hampering the realisation of developmental, economic and social goals.
"Political differences should not cause any blockade in economic life and life in general.
"Political and inter-party disputes ought to be settled in a constructive and democratic manner, in which activities of the government and its ministries play a special part," Milosevic said.
